# GLRMask

<!-- Generated by scripts/sync-guide.py from docs/content. Do not edit this output. -->

GLRMask is a grammar-constrained decoding library for high-throughput LLM serving. It is optimized for fast mask computation with extremely low tail latency, even for complex grammars.

GLRMask supports general context-free grammars, including ambiguous ones. It accepts JSON Schema, Lark, and GLRMask's native format: GLRM.

[Website](https://glrmask.com) · [Paper](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23273556)

#### Dynamic mode

GLRMask’s dynamic mode trades some mask-generation speed for lower cold-start latency. It is heavily based on [llguidance](https://github.com/guidance-ai/llguidance).

</picture>

[Explore Dynamic JSON results](https://glrmask.com/?dataset=json&mode=dynamic#benchmarks).

There was no CPU pinning or SMT sibling reservation, and checkpoint publication overlapped the benchmark. Saved telemetry cannot isolate scheduling effects; latency stabilization is not certified. Successful builds do not establish semantic correctness. All 9,558 JSON schemas were attempted: build errors are Dynamic 232, Static 233 and llguidance 1,226. Incorrect examples are 460 for each GLRMask mode and 100 for llguidance; runtime-error examples are 0 and 6 respectively. JavaScript attempts all 55 fixtures: all builds succeed, with 1 incorrect example per GLRMask mode and 4 for llguidance. Headline TBM excludes incomplete or nonaccepted valid trajectories; all outcomes remain in the raw records. This finite corpus does not establish full-language equivalence or whole-corpus dominance.

[Native AWS benchmark details](docs/benchmark-aws-2026-10-14.md). Historical [October 8 Mac JSON](docs/benchmark-cfa-2026-10-08.md) and [October 9 Mac JavaScript](docs/benchmark-javascript-2026-10-09.md) reports are retained with their original measurement protocols. These are source builds, not measurements of the published 0.2 packages.

## Getting started

### Installation

#### Python

```bash
python -m pip install glrmask
```

#### Rust

```bash
cargo add glrmask
```

#### Native C++ and Node.js

Native bindings are available for C++ and JavaScript/TypeScript on Node.js. The [C++ guide and C API](https://glrmask.com/api/cpp/) and [JavaScript and TypeScript guide](https://glrmask.com/api/javascript/) cover source builds, platform artifacts, ownership, composition, and the complete supported API. The Node.js addon runs the Rust engine directly; browser WebAssembly is a separate target.

### Usage

GLRMask has four core types:

- `Grammar`: a grammar, written as source text or built from an expression.
- `Module`: a grammar plus its extern bindings and any precompiled work. Can be saved and loaded.
- `Constraint`: a grammar compiled for a vocabulary, ready to use.
- `ConstraintState`: the state of one generated sequence.

### Python quickstart

```python
import glrmask

vocab = glrmask.Vocab.from_id_to_bytes({0: b"hello", 1: b" ", 2: b"world"})
grammar = glrmask.Grammar.from_lark('start: "hello" " " "world"')
constraint = grammar.compile(vocab)
state = constraint.start()
for token_id, expected in [(0, [True, False, False]),
                           (1, [False, True, False]),
                           (2, [False, False, True])]:
    assert state.mask().tolist() == expected
    assert state.commit_token(token_id)
assert state.is_accepting()
```

### Rust quickstart

```rust
use glrmask::{Grammar, Vocab};

fn main() -> glrmask::Result<()> {
    let vocab = Vocab::new(vec![
        (0, b"hello".to_vec()), (1, b" ".to_vec()), (2, b"world".to_vec()),
    ]);
    let grammar = Grammar::from_lark(r#"start: "hello" " " "world""#)?;
    let constraint = grammar.compile(&vocab)?;
    let mut state = constraint.start();
    for token_id in 0..3 {
        assert_eq!(state.mask()[0], 1 << token_id);
        assert!(state.commit_token(token_id));
    }
    assert!(state.is_accepting());
    Ok(())
}
```

### Composing grammars

A grammar can declare externs, named slots that you bind later: `extern grammar NAME` takes a grammar, and
`extern token NAME` takes token IDs. Each grammar keeps its own rules, including the whitespace it ignores. A `Module`
holds a grammar, its bindings and any precompiled work, so parts you reuse, such as each tool's schema, are compiled once:

```python
import glrmask

vocab = glrmask.Vocab.from_id_to_bytes({i: bytes([i]) for i in range(256)})
weather = glrmask.Module(glrmask.Grammar.from_json_schema(
    '{"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},'
    ' "required": ["city"], "additionalProperties": false}'))
weather.precompile(vocab)

call = glrmask.Module(glrmask.Grammar.from_glrm('''
    extern grammar ARGS
    start call
    nt call = "<weather>" ARGS "</weather>"
'''))
call.bind("ARGS", weather)
state = call.compile(vocab).start()
assert state.commit_bytes(b'<weather>{"city": "Perth"}</weather>')
assert state.is_accepting()
```

`Expr.choice`, `Expr.sequence` and `Expr.literal` combine grammars without writing a new one.

### End tokens

GLRMask has no end-token setting. To require an end-of-sequence token, put it after the grammar:
`Grammar.from_expr(Expr.sequence(grammar, TokenSet([eos_id])))`. `is_accepting()` says whether the text so far is a
complete match, and `is_terminated()` whether nothing more can be committed.

### Mask strategies

`MaskStrategy` trades compile time against mask speed. `ParserDwa` is slowest to compile, with the fastest masks;
`TokenTrie` is fastest to compile, with slower masks; `Auto`, the default, reuses precompiled work and otherwise uses
`ParserDwa`, or `TokenTrie` when that would be too large. `BoundaryMaskStrategy` makes the same choice where a grammar
meets a bound extern. Every strategy produces the same masks.

The [full guide](GUIDE.md) covers generation, composition, token sets, strategies, markers and errors.

## How it works

GLRMask maintains a GLR parser state for the generated prefix. A precomputed deterministic weighted automaton computes the next-token mask by reading each parser stack, intersecting Boolean vocabulary masks along each traversal and unioning alternative paths.

See [How it works](https://glrmask.com/implementation/) for the explanation and diagrams.
